Spidertrax's WHS007 at $135/pair is the most trusted spacer option for the JK — hub-centric design, 6061 aluminum billet, and they use the correct bore to sit fully on the hub face before the lug nuts load.

The hub-centric versus lug-centric distinction is the most important safety consideration in this category. Hub-centric spacers register on the wheel hub center bore (71.5mm on the JK) — the hub bore is what carries the vehicle's weight, and the lug nuts simply hold the assembly in place. Lug-centric spacers have a larger center bore and rely on the lug nuts to carry the load, which stresses the studs and causes vibration and premature wear. Every spacer listed here is hub-centric — do not purchase spacers that don't specify this. On budget spacers without hub registration, the vibration they induce at highway speed is often mistaken for a wheel balance or bearing issue.

Torque spec discipline matters on spacers. The spacer mounts to the hub on the factory studs; the wheel then mounts to the studs pressed into the spacer. Torque the spacer to the hub at 95–100 ft-lbs, then torque the wheel to the spacer at the same spec. After the first 50 miles, re-torque the spacer-to-hub interface — spacers can loosen slightly on initial seating. Thick spacers (1.75"+) may push the wheel far enough outboard to reduce effective thread engagement on the factory studs — check that you have at least one diameter of stud engagement past the wheel mounting surface, or purchase extended wheel studs.

Spacers make sense when they correct a specific fitment problem or when the alternative (new wheels) is disproportionately more expensive. If you're building from scratch or choosing wheels for a new tire size, buying wheels with the correct backspacing is cleaner and lighter than adding spacers. Spacers add approximately 2–4 lbs per corner in unsprung weight and introduce one more assembly interface that can loosen over time.
steps: Lift the vehicle and place on jack stands; remove the wheel.
Clean the hub face and wheel mounting surface — debris under the spacer causes runout.
Slide the spacer onto the hub, ensuring the center bore fully seats over the hub register.
Thread the spacer-to-hub lug nuts by hand before torquing.
Torque the spacer to the hub at 95–100 ft-lbs in a star pattern.
Mount the wheel to the spacer studs and torque to 95–100 ft-lbs.
Reinstall and repeat for all four corners.
Re-torque all spacer lug nuts after 50 miles.
pros: Solves backspacing fitment problems without purchasing new wheels
Hub-centric design eliminates vibration issues associated with lug-centric budget spacers
1.25" spacer typically costs less than replacing all four wheels with different backspacing
Wider track width slightly improves stability on tall builds with heavy gear

summary: The JK takes a 5x127mm (5x5") bolt pattern at 17"+ diameter for most builds with 33s or larger — the wheel choice that matters most for fitment is backspacing, not brand.
description:
The JK Wrangler's 5x127mm (5x5") bolt pattern and 71.5mm center bore are the starting specs every wheel purchase begins from. All listed options here are 17" — the most common size for 35" and 37" tires — though 18" wheels are available if tire selection at that diameter is acceptable to you. The Pro Comp Series 31 steel wheel at $89 is the rock-bottom entry: a steel stamped wheel that's heavy, durable, and completely replaceable without guilt when it contacts something hard on the trail. Steel wheels are the right call for any build where wheel damage is a real possibility — at $89 each, you replace the wheel, not your bank account. Method Race Wheels' 304 is the volume seller in cast alloy for the JK — lighter than steel, available in multiple finishes, proven fitment, and at $175 each they're well within reach of most builds.

Backspacing is the measurement that determines how far the wheel mounting surface sits inside the wheel barrel — it controls how much the tire sticks out from the fender and how close it gets to the inner suspension components. For most lifted JKs, the target backspacing range is 4.5" to 4.75". Less backspacing (less than 4.25") pushes the tire outward past the fender flare and creates a wide-track stance that looks aggressive but adds scrub radius and increases stress on wheel bearings and ball joints. More backspacing (5"+ on a lifted JK) tucks the tire inward and can cause interference with upper control arm brackets on lifts above 2.5". The Method 304 at 0mm offset sits in the correct zone; the Fuel Boost at -12mm offset pushes the wheel slightly further outward and may require confirming clearance on your specific lift height.

Beadlock wheels are for a specific use case: running tires at very low air pressure (5–10 psi) on rock terrain where the bead would otherwise unseat from the rim. The Raceline Renegade at $350 each is the entry point for a functional beadlock — the outer ring clamps the tire bead mechanically, eliminating bead separation risk at extreme pressure drops. Beadlock wheels are not street-legal in most jurisdictions because the outer ring bolts can loosen and cause catastrophic failure at highway speed — they require a torque check after every trail run. They're genuinely necessary only on a JK built specifically for low-pressure rock crawling; for overland and moderate trail use, a high-quality non-beadlock wheel at correct pressure is the better choice.
steps: Confirm the new wheel's bolt pattern (5x127), center bore (71.5mm), and backspacing before purchasing.
Mount and balance tires on the new wheels before installing on the vehicle.
Install wheels, threading all lug nuts by hand in a star pattern before applying torque.
Torque lug nuts to 95–100 ft-lbs in a star pattern (two passes recommended).
For beadlock wheels: torque the outer ring bolts to manufacturer spec (typically 12–14 ft-lbs) before first use and recheck after 50 miles.
Re-torque all lug nuts after 50–100 miles on new wheels.

cons: Incorrect backspacing is the most common JK wheel fitment error — measure before ordering
Beadlock wheels require post-trail ring bolt torque checks — neglecting this is a safety hazard
Steel wheels add 5–8 lbs each over cast alloy — noticeable in unsprung weight and fuel economy
